title: Custom Engine Rebuild Wiring and Swap Agent
oneLine: I used an AI coding agent to research and document a 1998-engine-into-1988-truck swap, and built the verification system that makes its output safe to act on in the real world.

intro: I'm swapping a rebuilt, supercharged 1998 Toyota V6 into a 1988 4Runner, and I used an AI coding agent for the research, documentation and tooling. Because a wrong pin or torque spec costs real hardware, I built a verification process around the model: factory-manual sources only, a line-by-line audit of its output, meter readings as ground truth, and a build that fails on bad data.
The audit graded 207 lines of AI-written instructions and found 44 that needed fixing, none of which a quick read would have caught.

This is applied AI: agent workflow, evaluation and verification. I did not train or fine-tune a model. The build is also still in progress. 23 of the 65 jobs on the checklist are done, and the engine has not run in the truck yet.

sections.label: Problem
sections.title: An AI agent that isn't allowed to guess
body: The engineering problem: the truck keeps its original 5-speed manual and its original gauges, and the 1998 engine runs on a plug-in standalone ECU. So the electronics of a 1998 engine have to live inside a 1988 truck, and the signals between them have to be traced across two sets of factory wiring diagrams.

The AI problem is the one every applied-AI team has: how do you use a language model on a task where a confident wrong answer is expensive? Here a wrong pin number can destroy an engine computer and a wrong torque spec can destroy an engine. I couldn't take the model's word for anything, so I designed a process around it.
sections.callout: Nothing gets used because the model said it. Every number has to trace back to a factory manual page or a meter reading on this truck.

sections.label: Method
sections.title: Six checks between the model and the truck

cards.title: Grounding
cards.body: The agent may only use Toyota's factory service manuals and wiring diagrams as sources. Every spec carries the manual page code so I can check it by hand.

cards.title: Evaluation
cards.body: A second pass re-read the manual and graded every line of the AI-written build guide as MATCH, FIX, OMISSION or LABEL. The result is in the next section.

cards.title: Verifying outside knowledge
cards.body: The wiring plan started from a well-known forum write-up. Before using it, the agent checked 53 entries pin by pin against Toyota's diagrams. It found three wrong function labels and a swapped pair of pins. One wire labelled "not used" was really the main power feed for the airflow sensor, idle valve and oxygen-sensor heaters.

cards.title: Ground truth from the truck
cards.body: Documents are checked against meter readings I take on the truck. When a document and the meter disagree, the meter wins.

cards.title: Explicit uncertainty
cards.body: Anything not confirmed by a manual page or a measurement is tagged UNVERIFIED and comes with the exact test that would settle it. The example below is one of those tags.

cards.title: One source of truth, and a build that can fail
cards.body: 143 connector pins live in one JSON file. Python generators produce the connector diagrams, the printed garage binder and the website from the same notes.

code.file: An UNVERIFIED tag, as quoted on the live case study
code.text:
N5-1 is most likely the fuel pump output. UNVERIFIED.
Check: key ON, ground N5-8 → N5-1 reads 12 V.

sections.label: Audit
sections.title: The first draft was 79% right
body: The agent wrote the first draft of the engine build guide from the manual. Then a second pass re-read the manual and graded the guide line by line. Across 207 lines: 163 match, 26 fix, 15 omission, 3 label.

So the first draft was 79% right, and the 21% that wasn't was the dangerous kind: steps missing from a sequence, cautions left out, cross-references to the wrong step. No torque, clearance or angle contradicted the manual. All the fixes were applied.

Lines
What it means

The numbers were right, but steps, cautions or specs from the manual were missing

sections.label: Pipeline
sections.title: From manual page to garage floor
body: The notes are the only thing the outputs are built from. There are 18 research notes, each answering one question: the power budget, the gauge signals, every plug on the harness, a full wiring audit, and so on.
The site build fails if a private detail or a copyrighted manual file would be published, or if any link is broken. The check below is the end of the build script.

flow.summary: Factory manuals, wiring diagrams and meter readings feed research notes and one pin data file. Audits and pin-by-pin checks correct the notes. Python generators turn the notes into connector diagrams, a printed binder and the website. The site build stops if it finds a private detail, a manual file or a broken link.

    broken = link_check()

sections.label: Failures
sections.title: What went wrong
body: The checks exist because they kept finding things.

cards.title: 44 of 207 lines needed work
cards.body: That is the score for the first AI draft before any checking. It was mostly right, with the errors in places a quick read would not catch.

cards.title: A bug in the page generator
cards.body: The audit caught a bug in the page generator: four spec chips linked to page 1 of the manual instead of their own page.

cards.title: The manual that didn't cover the engine
cards.body: The notes assumed a 1988 repair manual covered the V6's wiring. Reading it page by page showed it covers only the four-cylinder. The correction is logged and the affected items are still marked open.

cards.title: When the sources disagree
cards.body: Two pages of the same factory manual imply opposite polarity for one signal. The note doesn't pick one. It specifies a bench test that decides it.
